claim: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are host-encoded antibiotics that combat invading microorganisms.
source: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are host-encoded antibiotics that combat invading microorganisms.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by established scientific knowledge about AMPs.

claim: In vitro studies have shown AMPs kill bacteria and fungi at physiological concentrations.
source: In vitro studies have shown AMPs kill bacteria and fungi at physiological concentrations, but little validation has been done in vivo.
evidence: This claim references prior in vitro studies, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Little validation of AMP antimicrobial activity has been done in vivo.
source: In vitro studies have shown AMPs kill bacteria and fungi at physiological concentrations, but little validation has been done in vivo.
evidence: This statement reflects the gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: The study utilized CRISPR gene editing to delete most known immune-inducible AMPs of Drosophila.
source: We utilized CRISPR gene editing to delete most known immune-inducible AMPs of Drosophila, namely: 4 Attacins, 2 Diptericins, Drosocin, Drosomycin, Metchnikowin and Defensin.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Ten AMP genes were deleted in Drosophila: 4 Attacins, 2 Diptericins, Drosocin, Drosomycin, Metchnikowin and Defensin.
source: We utilized CRISPR gene editing to delete most known immune-inducible AMPs of Drosophila, namely: 4 Attacins, 2 Diptericins, Drosocin, Drosomycin, Metchnikowin and Defensin.
evidence: This lists the specific genes deleted in the study.

claim: Drosophila AMPs act primarily against Gram-negative bacteria and fungi.
source: We found that Drosophila AMPs act primarily against Gram-negative bacteria and fungi, contributing either additively or synergistically.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the survival experiments and bacterial load measurements.

claim: Drosophila AMPs contribute either additively or synergistically to host defense.
source: We found that Drosophila AMPs act primarily against Gram-negative bacteria and fungi, contributing either additively or synergistically.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of compound mutants showing additive and synergistic effects.

claim: Certain AMPs contribute the bulk of microbicidal activity against specific pathogens.
source: We also describe remarkable specificity wherein certain AMPs contribute the bulk of microbicidal activity against specific pathogens, providing functional demonstrations of highly specific AMP-pathogen interactions in an in vivo setting.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the specific interactions observed with Diptericins and P. rettgeri, and Drosocin and E. cloacae.

claim: The study provides functional demonstrations of highly specific AMP-pathogen interactions in an in vivo setting.
source: We also describe remarkable specificity wherein certain AMPs contribute the bulk of microbicidal activity against specific pathogens, providing functional demonstrations of highly specific AMP-pathogen interactions in an in vivo setting.
evidence: This is supported by the survival experiments showing specific AMP requirements for different pathogens.

claim: The existence of multiple effectors that redundantly contribute to host resistance has hampered their functional characterization by genetic approaches.
source: The existence of multiple effectors that redundantly contribute to host resistance has hampered their functional characterization by genetic approaches (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: AMPs are small, cationic, usually amphipathic peptides that contribute to innate immune defence in plants and animals.
source: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are small, cationic, usually amphipathic peptides that contribute to innate immune defence in plants and animals (Imler and Bulet, 2005; Guaní-Guerra et al., 2010; Rolff and Schmid-Hempel, 2016).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: AMPs display potent antimicrobial activity in vitro by disrupting negatively charged microbial membranes.
source: They display potent antimicrobial activity in vitro by disrupting negatively charged microbial membranes, but AMPs can also target specific microbial processes (Park et al., 1998; Kragol et al., 2001; Rahnamaeian et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: AMPs can target specific microbial processes.
source: They display potent antimicrobial activity in vitro by disrupting negatively charged microbial membranes, but AMPs can also target specific microbial processes (Park et al., 1998; Kragol et al., 2001; Rahnamaeian et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: AMP expression is induced to very high levels upon challenge to provide microbicidal concentrations in the μM range.
source: Their expression is induced to very high levels upon challenge to provide microbicidal concentrations in the μM range.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about AMP expression patterns.

claim: There are currently seven well-characterized families of inducible AMPs in D. melanogaster.
source: There are currently seven well-characterized families of inducible AMPs in D. melanogaster, but we note that many genes encoding small peptides are strongly upregulated upon infection and are awaiting description (De Gregorio et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Many genes encoding small peptides are strongly upregulated upon infection in Drosophila and are awaiting description.
source: There are currently seven well-characterized families of inducible AMPs in D. melanogaster, but we note that many genes encoding small peptides are strongly upregulated upon infection and are awaiting description (De Gregorio et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Drosomycin and Metchnikowin show antifungal activity.
source: Drosomycin and Metchnikowin show antifungal activity (Fehlbaum et al., 1994; Levashina et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Cecropins and Defensin have both antibacterial and some antifungal activities.
source: Cecropins (four inducible genes) and Defensin have both antibacterial and some antifungal activities (Hultmark et al., 1980; Ekengren and Hultmark, 1999; Cociancich et al., 1993; Tzou et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Drosocin, Attacins and Diptericins primarily exhibit antibacterial activity.
source: and Drosocin, Attacins (four genes) and Diptericins (two genes) primarily exhibit antibacterial activity (Kragol et al., 2001; Asling et al., 1995; Cudic et al., 1999; Hedengren et al., 2000; Bulet et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: AMPs are produced either locally at various surface epithelia in contact with environmental microbes or secreted systemically into the hemolymph.
source: In Drosophila, these AMPs are produced either locally at various surface epithelia in contact with environmental microbes (Tzou et al., 2000; Basset et al., 2000; Gendrin et al., 2009), or secreted systemically into the hemolymph, the insect blood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: During systemic infection, 14 antimicrobial peptides are strongly induced in the fat body.
source: During systemic infection, these 14 antimicrobial peptides are strongly induced in the fat body, an organ analogous to the mammalian liver.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Drosophila immune response.

claim: The systemic production of AMPs is regulated at the transcriptional level by two NF-κB pathways, the Toll and Imd pathways.
source: The systemic production of AMPs is regulated at the transcriptional level by two NF-κB pathways, the Toll and Imd pathways, which are activated by different classes of microbes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Drosophila immune signaling.

claim: The Toll pathway is predominantly responsive to Gram-positive bacteria and fungi.
source: The Toll pathway is predominantly responsive to Gram-positive bacteria and fungi, and accordingly plays a major role in defence against these microbes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Drosophila immune signaling.

claim: The Imd pathway is activated by Gram-negative bacteria and a subset of Gram-positive bacteria with DAP-type peptidoglycan.
source: In contrast, the Imd pathway is activated by Gram-negative bacteria and a subset of Gram-positive bacteria with DAP-type peptidoglycan, and mutations affecting this pathway cause profound susceptibility to Gram-negative bacteria (De Gregorio et al., 2002; Lemaitre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mutations affecting the Imd pathway cause profound susceptibility to Gram-negative bacteria.
source: In contrast, the Imd pathway is activated by Gram-negative bacteria and a subset of Gram-positive bacteria with DAP-type peptidoglycan, and mutations affecting this pathway cause profound susceptibility to Gram-negative bacteria (De Gregorio et al., 2002; Lemaitre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Transgenic flies overexpressing a single AMP show improved host defence.
source: While a critical role of AMPs in Drosophila host defence is supported by transgenic flies overexpressing a single AMP (Tzou et al., 2002), the specific contributions of each of these AMPs has not been tested.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss-of-function mutants for most AMP genes were not previously available due to their small size.
source: Indeed loss-of-function mutants for most AMP genes were not previously available due to their small size, making them difficult to mutate before the advent of CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the current study.

claim: Flies lacking a set of uncharacterized Toll-responsive peptides (Bomanins) succumb to infection by Gram-positive bacteria and fungi at rates similar to Toll-deficient mutants.
source: Strikingly, Clemmons et al. (2015) recently reported that flies lacking a set of uncharacterized Toll-responsive peptides (named Bomanins) succumb to infection by Gram-positive bacteria and fungi at rates similar to Toll-deficient mutants (Clemmons et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Synthesized Bomanins do not display antimicrobial activity in vitro.
source: This provocatively suggests that Bomanins, and not AMPs, might be the predominant effectors downstream of the Toll pathway; yet synthesized Bomanins do not display antimicrobial activity in vitro (Lindsay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Five single gene mutations were generated affecting Defensin (DefSK3), Attacin C (AttCMi), Metchnikowin (MtkR1), Attacin D (AttDSK1) and Drosomycin (DrsR1).
source: These include five single gene mutations affecting Defensin (DefSK3), Attacin C (AttCMi), Metchnikowin (MtkR1), Attacin D (AttDSK1) and Drosomycin (DrsR1), respectively
evidence: This describes the mutants generated in the study.

claim: Two small deletions were generated removing both Diptericins DptA and DptB (DptSK1), or the gene cluster containing Drosocin, and Attacins AttA and AttB (Dro-AttABSK2).
source: and two small deletions removing both Diptericins DptA and DptB (DptSK1), or the gene cluster containing Drosocin, and Attacins AttA and AttB (Dro-AttABSK2).
evidence: This describes the mutants generated in the study.

claim: All mutations/deletions were made using the CRISPR editing approach with the exception of Attacin C and the Drosomycin and Metchnikowin deletions.
source: All mutations/deletions were made using the CRISPR editing approach with the exception of Attacin C, which was disrupted by insertion of a Minos transposable element (Bellen et al., 2011), and the Drosomycin and Metchnikowin deletions generated by homologous recombination (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the methods used to generate mutants.

claim: Attacin C was disrupted by insertion of a Minos transposable element.
source: All mutations/deletions were made using the CRISPR editing approach with the exception of Attacin C, which was disrupted by insertion of a Minos transposable element (Bellen et al., 2011), and the Drosomycin and Metchnikowin deletions generated by homologous recombination (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the Attacin C mutant, supported by a citation.

claim: Drosomycin and Metchnikowin deletions were generated by homologous recombination.
source: All mutations/deletions were made using the CRISPR editing approach with the exception of Attacin C, which was disrupted by insertion of a Minos transposable element (Bellen et al., 2011), and the Drosomycin and Metchnikowin deletions generated by homologous recombination (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate these mutants.

claim: An individual Drosocin mutant (DroSK4) was generated to disentangle the role of Drosocin and AttA/AttB in the Dro-AttABSK2 deletion.
source: To disentangle the role of Drosocin and AttA/AttB in the Dro-AttABSK2 deletion, we also generated an individual Drosocin mutant (DroSK4); for complete information, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This describes an additional mutant generated for the study.

claim: Mutations were isogenized for at least seven generations into the w1118 DrosDel isogenic genetic background.
source: We then isogenized these mutations for at least seven generations into the w1118 DrosDel isogenic genetic background (Ryder et al., 2004) (iso w1118).
evidence: This describes the genetic background preparation, supported by a citation.

claim: Seven independent mutations were recombined into a background lacking these 10 inducible AMPs referred to as 'ΔAMPs.'
source: Then, we recombined these seven independent mutations into a background lacking these 10 inducible AMPs referred to as 'ΔAMPs.'
evidence: This describes the generation of the compound mutant.

claim: ΔAMPs flies were viable and showed no morphological defects.
source: ΔAMPs flies were viable and showed no morphological defects.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: MALDI-TOF analysis revealed the presence of peaks induced upon challenge corresponding to AMPs in wild-type but not ΔAMPs flies.
source: This analysis revealed the presence of peaks induced upon challenge corresponding to AMPs in wild-type but not ΔAMPs flies.
evidence: This is supported by the MALDI-TOF data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Induction of most other immune-induced molecules (IMs) was unaffected in ΔAMPs flies.
source: Importantly, it also confirmed that induction of most other immune-induced molecules (IMs) (Uttenweiler-Joseph et al., 1998), was unaffected in ΔAMPs flies (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the MALDI-TOF data shown in Figure 1B and a citation.

claim: Two IMs, IM7 and IM21, were not observed in ΔAMPs flies.
source: Of note, we failed to observe two IMs, IM7 and IM21, in our ΔAMPs flies, suggesting that these unknown peptides are secondary products of AMP genes.
evidence: This is an observation from the MALDI-TOF analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IM7 and IM21 are likely secondary products of AMP genes.
source: Of note, we failed to observe two IMs, IM7 and IM21, in our ΔAMPs flies, suggesting that these unknown peptides are secondary products of AMP genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of these molecules in ΔAMPs flies.

claim: Toll and Imd NF-κB signaling pathways were intact in ΔAMPs flies.
source: We further confirmed that Toll and Imd NF-κB signaling pathways were intact in ΔAMPs flies by measuring the expression of target genes of these pathways (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Drosophila AMPs are not signaling molecules required for Toll or Imd pathway activity.
source: This demonstrates that Drosophila AMPs are not signaling molecules required for Toll or Imd pathway activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the intact signaling in ΔAMPs flies.

claim: After clean injury, ΔAMPs flies survive as wild-type.
source: After clean injury, ΔAMPs flies survive as wild-type (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No defect in melanization was found in ΔAMPs flies.
source: We found no defect in melanization (χ2, p=0.34, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) as both adults and larvae strongly melanize the cuticle following clean injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by melanization assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: Rapid formation of clot fibers was visualized ex vivo in hemolymph of both wild-type and ΔAMPs larvae.
source: Furthermore, we visualized the rapid formation of clot fibers ex vivo using the hanging drop assay and PNA staining (Scherfer et al., 2004) in hemolymph of both wild-type and ΔAMPs larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by clotting assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and a citation.

claim: Hemocyte counting did not reveal any deficiency in hemocyte populations of ΔAMPs larvae.
source: Hemocyte counting (i.e. crystal cells, FACS) did not reveal any deficiency in hemocyte populations of ΔAMPs larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F, and not shown).
evidence: This is supported by hemocyte counting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: Drosophila AMPs are primarily immune effectors, and not regulators of innate immunity.
source: Altogether, our study suggests that Drosophila AMPs are primarily immune effectors, and not regulators of innate immunity.
evidence: This is inferred from the various functional assays showing no defects in immune signaling or other immune processes.

claim: ΔAMPs flies were extremely susceptible to all Gram-negative pathogens tested.
source: Globally, ΔAMPs flies were extremely susceptible to all Gram-negative pathogens tested (Figure 2, light blue plots).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The susceptibility of AMP-deficient flies to Gram-negative bacteria largely mirrored that of RelE20 flies.
source: The susceptibility of AMP-deficient flies to Gram-negative bacteria largely mirrored that of RelE20 flies.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of survival curves in Figure 2.

claim: For all Gram-negative infections tested, ΔAMPs flies show a higher bacterial count at 18 hr post-infection indicating that AMPs actively inhibit bacterial growth.
source: For all Gram-negative infections tested, ΔAMPs flies show a higher bacterial count at 18 hr post-infection (hpi) indicating that AMPs actively inhibit bacterial growth, as expected of 'antimicrobial peptides' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bacterial growth in ΔAMPs flies radiates from the wound site until spreading systemically.
source: Use of GFP-expressing bacteria show that bacterial growth in ΔAMPs flies radiates from the wound site until spreading systemically (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: AMPs are major players in resistance to Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Collectively, the use of AMP-deficient flies reveals that AMPs are major players in resistance to Gram-negative bacteria, and likely constitute an essential component of the Imd pathway's contribution for survival against these germs.
evidence: This is inferred from the high susceptibility of ΔAMPs flies to Gram-negative bacteria.

claim: AMPs likely constitute an essential component of the Imd pathway's contribution for survival against Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Collectively, the use of AMP-deficient flies reveals that AMPs are major players in resistance to Gram-negative bacteria, and likely constitute an essential component of the Imd pathway's contribution for survival against these germs.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between ΔAMPs and RelE20 susceptibility.

claim: Resistance to Gram-positive bacteria and fungi in Drosophila is mostly mediated by the Toll pathway.
source: Previous studies have shown that resistance to Gram-positive bacteria and fungi in Drosophila is mostly mediated by the Toll pathway, although the Imd pathway also contributes to some extent (Lemaitre et al., 1997; Leulier et al., 2000; Rutschmann et al., 2002; Tanji et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A deletion removing ten uncharacterized Bomanins (BomΔ55C) induces a strong susceptibility to both Gram-positive bacteria and fungi.
source: Moreover, a deletion removing ten uncharacterized Bomanins (BomΔ55C) induces a strong susceptibility to both Gram-positive bacteria and fungi (Clemmons et al., 2015), suggesting that Bomanins are major players downstream of Toll in the defence against these germs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ΔAMPs flies display only weak or no increased susceptibility to infection with Gram-positive bacterial species.
source: We observed that ΔAMPs flies display only weak or no increased susceptibility to infection with these Gram-positive bacterial species, as ΔAMPs survival rates were closer to the wild-type than to spzrm7 mutants lacking a functional Toll pathway (Figure 2, orange plots), with the exception of S. aureus.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: BomΔ55C mutants consistently phenocopied spzrm7 flies in Gram-positive bacterial infections.
source: Meanwhile, BomΔ55C mutants consistently phenocopied spzrm7 flies, confirming the important contribution of these peptides in defence against Gram-positive bacteria (Clemmons et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 2 and a citation.

claim: ΔAMPs flies were more susceptible to fungal infections with B. bassiana, A. fumigatus, and C. albicans, but not M. anisopliae.
source: ΔAMPs flies were more susceptible to fungal infections with B. bassiana, A. fumigatus, and C. albicans, but not M. anisopliae (Figure 2, yellow plots).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In all fungal infection instances, BomΔ55C mutants were as or more susceptible to fungal infection than ΔAMPs flies.
source: In all instances, BomΔ55C mutants were as or more susceptible to fungal infection than ΔAMPs flies, approaching Toll-deficient mutant levels.
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 2.

claim: AMPs are major immune effectors in defence against Gram-negative bacteria and have a less essential role in defence against bacteria and fungi.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrate that AMPs are major immune effectors in defence against Gram-negative bacteria and have a less essential role in defence against bacteria and fungi.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential susceptibility patterns observed across different pathogen types.

claim: Cooperation of AMPs to potentiate their microbicidal activity has been suggested by numerous in vitro approaches.
source: Indeed, cooperation of AMPs to potentiate their microbicidal activity has been suggested by numerous in vitro approaches (Rahnamaeian et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2016; Mohan et al., 2014), but rarely in an in vivo context (Zanchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Group C flies lacking Metchnikowin and Drosomycin were more susceptible to C. albicans infection with a survival rate similar to ΔAMPs flies.
source: Consistent with this, Group C flies lacking Metchnikowin and Drosomycin were more susceptible to infection (p<0.001 relative to iso w1118) with a survival rate similar to ΔAMPs flies (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AC-deficient flies that also lack Defensin survived better than Group C-deficient flies in C. albicans infection.
source: Curiously, AC-deficient flies that also lack Defensin survived better than Group C-deficient flies (Log-Rank p=0.014).
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 3A.

claim: Both MtkR1 and DrsR1 individual mutants were somewhat susceptible to C. albicans infection.
source: We found that both MtkR1 and DrsR1 individual mutants were somewhat susceptible to infection, but notably only Mtk; Drs compound mutants reached ΔAMPs levels of susceptibility (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only Mtk; Drs compound mutants reached ΔAMPs levels of susceptibility to C. albicans.
source: We found that both MtkR1 and DrsR1 individual mutants were somewhat susceptible to infection, but notably only Mtk; Drs compound mutants reached ΔAMPs levels of susceptibility (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The co-occurring loss of resistance to C. albicans by Metchnikowin and Drosomycin appears to be primarily additive.
source: This co-occurring loss of resistance appears to be primarily additive (Mutant, Cox Hazard Ratio (HR), p-value: MtkR1, HR =+1.17, p=0.008; DrsR1, HR =+1.85, p<0.001; Mtk*Drs, HR = −0.80, p=0.116).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: Group C deficient flies eventually succumb to uncontrolled C. albicans growth.
source: We observed that Group C deficient flies eventually succumb to uncontrolled C. albicans growth by monitoring yeast titre, indicating that these AMPs indeed act by suppressing yeast growth (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by fungal load data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The study provides an in vivo validation of the potent antifungal activities of Metchnikowin and Drosomycin.
source: In conclusion, our study provides an in vivo validation of the potent antifungal activities of Metchnikowin and Drosomycin (Fehlbaum et al., 1994; Levashina et al., 1995), and highlights a clear example of additive cooperation of AMPs.
evidence: This is supported by the survival and fungal load data, along with citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: Group B mutants lacking Drosocin, the two Diptericins, and the four Attacins, were as susceptible to P. burhodogranariea infection as ΔAMPs flies.
source: We found that Group B mutants lacking Drosocin, the two Diptericins, and the four Attacins, were as susceptible to infection as ΔAMPs flies (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Flies lacking the antifungal peptides Drosomycin and Metchnikowin (Group C) resisted P. burhodogranariea infection as wild-type.
source: while flies lacking the antifungal peptides Drosomycin and Metchnikowin (Toll-regulated, Group C) resisted the infection as wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 4A.

claim: Flies lacking Defensin (Group A) showed an intermediate susceptibility to P. burhodogranariea.
source: Flies lacking Defensin (Group A) showed an intermediate susceptibility, but behave as wild-type in the additional absence of Toll Group C peptides (Group AC).
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutants for Drosocin alone (DroSK4), or the DiptericinA/B deficiency were not susceptible to P. burhodogranariea.
source: We observed that mutants for Drosocin alone (DroSK4), or the DiptericinA/B deficiency were not susceptible to this bacterium (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Compound mutants lacking Drosocin and Attacins A, B, C, and D displayed an intermediate susceptibility to P. burhodogranariea.
source: Interestingly, we found that compound mutants lacking Drosocin and Attacins A, B, C, and D (Figure 4B: 'ΔDro, ΔAtt'), or Drosocin and Diptericins DptA and DptB ('ΔDro, ΔDpt') displayed an intermediate susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Compound mutants lacking Drosocin and Diptericins DptA and DptB displayed an intermediate susceptibility to P. burhodogranariea.
source: Interestingly, we found that compound mutants lacking Drosocin and Attacins A, B, C, and D (Figure 4B: 'ΔDro, ΔAtt'), or Drosocin and Diptericins DptA and DptB ('ΔDro, ΔDpt') displayed an intermediate susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only the Group B mutants lacking Drosocin, all Attacins, and both Diptericins phenocopied ΔAMPs flies in P. burhodogranariea infection.
source: Only the Group B mutants lacking Drosocin, all Attacins, and both Diptericins (ΔDro, ΔAtt, ΔDpt) phenocopied ΔAMPs flies (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Synergistic statistical interactions were observed upon co-occurring loss of Attacins and Diptericins in P. burhodogranariea infection.
source: with synergistic statistical interactions observed upon co-occurring loss of Attacins and Diptericins (ΔAtt*ΔDpt: HR =+1.45, p<0.001)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: By 6hpi, bacterial titres of individual flies showed significant differences in the most susceptible genotypes to P. burhodogranariea.
source: By 6hpi, bacterial titres of individual flies already showed significant differences in the most susceptible genotypes (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Several Imd-responsive AMPs, notably Drosocin, Attacins, and Diptericins, jointly contribute to defence against P. burhodogranariea infection.
source: Collectively, the use of various compound mutants reveals that several Imd-responsive AMPs, notably Drosocin, Attacins, and Diptericins, jointly contribute to defence against P. burhodogranariea infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the compound mutant survival data.

claim: A strong susceptibility of Group B flies was also observed upon infection with Ecc15.
source: A strong susceptibility of Group B flies was also observed upon infection with Ecc15, another Gram-negative bacterium commonly used to infect flies (Neyen et al., 2014) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B ).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and a citation.

claim: Previous studies have shown a correlation between susceptibility to P. rettgeri and a polymorphism in the Diptericin A gene.
source: We were especially interested by this bacterium as previous studies (Unckless et al., 2015; Unckless and Lazzaro, 2016) have shown a correlation between susceptibility to P. rettgeri and a polymorphism in the Diptericin A gene pointing to a specific AMP-pathogen interaction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Only loss of Group B AMPs was needed to reach the susceptibility of ΔAMPs and RelE20 flies to P. rettgeri.
source: Use of compound mutants revealed only loss of Group B AMPs was needed to reach the susceptibility of ΔAMPs and RelE20 flies (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The sole Diptericin A/B deficiency caused susceptibility similar to Group B, ΔAMPs, and RelE20 flies to P. rettgeri.
source: Use of individual mutant lines, however, revealed a pattern overtly different from P. burhodogranariea, as the sole Diptericin A/B deficiency caused susceptibility similar to Group B, ΔAMPs, and RelE20 flies (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: DptA RNAi confirmed the susceptibility to P. rettgeri.
source: We further confirmed this susceptibility using a DptA RNAi construct (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi survival data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Flies carrying the DptSK1 mutation over a deficiency (Df(2R)Exel6067) were highly susceptible to P. rettgeri.
source: Moreover, flies carrying the DptSK1 mutation over a deficiency (Df(2R)Exel6067) were also highly susceptible to P. rettgeri (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Flies that were heterozygotes for DptSK1 or the Df(2R)Exel6067 were markedly susceptible to infection with P. rettgeri.
source: Interestingly, flies that were heterozygotes for DptSK1 or the Df(2R)Exel6067 that still have one copy of the two Diptericins were markedly susceptible to infection with P. rettgeri (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A full transcriptional output of Diptericin is required over the course of the infection to resist P. rettgeri.
source: This indicates that a full transcriptional output of Diptericin is required over the course of the infection to resist P. rettgeri (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is inferred from the heterozygote susceptibility and supported by expression data in Figure 5E.

claim: Only the Diptericin gene family provides the full AMP-based contribution to defence against P. rettgeri.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that only the Diptericin gene family, amongst the many AMPs regulated by the Imd pathway, provides the full AMP-based contribution to defence against this bacterium.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data showing Diptericin-specific effects.

claim: ΔAMPs+Dpt flies (lacking all AMPs except DptA and DptB) have the same survival rate as wild-type flies against P. rettgeri.
source: Strikingly, ΔAMPs+Dpt flies have the same survival rate as wild-type flies, further emphasizing the specificity of this interaction (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Bacterial counts confirm that the susceptibility of Diptericin mutants arises from an inability of the host to suppress P. rettgeri growth.
source: Bacterial counts confirm that the susceptibility of these Diptericin mutants arises from an inability of the host to suppress bacterial growth (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Diptericins are critical to resist P. rettgeri.
source: Collectively, our study shows that Diptericins are critical to resist P. rettgeri, while they play an important but less essential role in defence against P. burhodogranariea infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data across different Providencia species.

claim: Diptericins play an important but less essential role in defence against P. burhodogranariea infection.
source: Collectively, our study shows that Diptericins are critical to resist P. rettgeri, while they play an important but less essential role in defence against P. burhodogranariea infection.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the survival data for P. rettgeri and P. burhodogranariea.

claim: An exclusive role for Diptericins was also found for P. stuartii.
source: An exclusive role for Diptericins was also found for the more virulent P. stuartii (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), but not for other Providencia species tested (P. burhodogranariea, P. alcalifaciens, P. sneebia, P. vermicola) (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Group B flies were susceptible to E. cloacae.
source: Use of compound mutants revealed that alone, Group B flies were already susceptible to E. cloacae.
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 6A.

claim: Group AB flies reached ΔAMPs levels of susceptibility to E. cloacae.
source: Meanwhile, Group AB flies reached ΔAMPs levels of susceptibility, while Group A and Group C flies resisted as wild-type (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The high susceptibility of Group AB flies to E. cloacae results from a synergistic statistical interaction amongst Group A (Defensin) and Group B peptides.
source: The high susceptibility of Group AB flies results from a synergistic statistical interaction amongst Group A (Defensin) and Group B peptides in defence against E. cloacae (A*B, HR =+2.55, p=0.003).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: Loss of Drosocin alone (DroSK4) recapitulates the susceptibility of Group B flies to E. cloacae.
source: Use of individual mutant lines revealed that mutants for Drosocin alone (DroSK4) or the Drosocin-Attacin A/B deficiency (Dro-AttABSK2), but not AttC, AttD, nor DptSK1 (not shown), recapitulate the susceptibility observed in Group B flies (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Drosocin-Attacin A/B deficiency (Dro-AttABSK2) recapitulates the susceptibility of Group B flies to E. cloacae.
source: Use of individual mutant lines revealed that mutants for Drosocin alone (DroSK4) or the Drosocin-Attacin A/B deficiency (Dro-AttABSK2), but not AttC, AttD, nor DptSK1 (not shown), recapitulate the susceptibility observed in Group B flies (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At 18 hpi, both DroSK4 and ΔAMPs flies had significantly higher bacterial loads of E. cloacae compared to wild-type flies.
source: At 18 hpi, both DroSK4 and ΔAMPs flies had significantly higher bacterial loads compared to wild-type flies, while RelE20 mutants were already moribund with much higher bacterial loads (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The deletion of Drosocin alone alters the fly's ability to control the otherwise avirulent E. cloacae upon inoculations using OD = 200 or even OD = 10.
source: Indeed, the deletion of Drosocin alone alters the fly's ability to control the otherwise avirulent E. cloacae upon inoculations using OD = 200 (~39,000 bacteria, Figure 6A–C) or even OD = 10 (~7000 bacteria, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6A-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The high susceptibility of Drosocin mutant flies to E. cloacae was confirmed in various contexts including transheterozygotes, alternate genetic backgrounds, and RNAi.
source: We confirmed the high susceptibility of Drosocin mutant flies to E. cloacae in various contexts: transheterozygote flies carrying DroSK4 over a Drosocin deficiency (Df(2R)BSC858) that also lacks flanking genes including AttA and AttB ((Figure 6D), the Dro SK4 mutations in an alternate genetic background (yw, Figure 6E), and, Drosocin RNAi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6D-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Two highly specific AMP-pathogen interactions were recovered: Diptericins are essential to combat P. rettgeri infection, while Drosocin is paramount to surviving E. cloacae infection.
source: Thus, we recovered two highly specific AMP-pathogen interactions: Diptericins are essential to combat P. rettgeri infection, while Drosocin is paramount to surviving E. cloacae infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data showing specific requirements for these AMPs.

claim: ΔAMPs flies were perfectly healthy and have an otherwise wild-type immune response.
source: A striking first finding is that ΔAMPs flies were perfectly healthy and have an otherwise wild-type immune response.
evidence: This is supported by the various functional assays showing normal immune signaling and other processes.

claim: In contrast to mammals, Drosophila AMPs are not likely to function as signaling molecules.
source: This indicates that in contrast to mammals (van Wetering et al., 2002), these Drosophila AMPs are not likely to function as signaling molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the intact immune signaling in ΔAMPs flies and supported by a citation.

claim: Most flies lacking a single AMP family exhibited a higher susceptibility to certain pathogens consistent with their in vitro activity.
source: Using a systemic mode of infection that induces AMP expression in the fat body and hemocytes, we found that most flies lacking a single AMP family exhibited a higher susceptibility to certain pathogens consistent with their in vitro activity.
evidence: This is supported by the survival data for individual mutants.

claim: Activity of Diptericins against P. rettgeri was found.
source: We found activity of Diptericins against P. rettgeri, Drosocin against E. cloacae, Drosomycin and Metchnikowin against C. albicans, and Defensin against P. burhodogranariea.
evidence: This is supported by the survival data for these specific AMP-pathogen combinations.

claim: Activity of Drosocin against E. cloacae was found.
source: We found activity of Diptericins against P. rettgeri, Drosocin against E. cloacae, Drosomycin and Metchnikowin against C. albicans, and Defensin against P. burhodogranariea.
evidence: This is supported by the survival data for these specific AMP-pathogen combinations.

claim: Activity of Drosomycin and Metchnikowin against C. albicans was found.
source: We found activity of Diptericins against P. rettgeri, Drosocin against E. cloacae, Drosomycin and Metchnikowin against C. albicans, and Defensin against P. burhodogranariea.
evidence: This is supported by the survival data for these specific AMP-pathogen combinations.

claim: Activity of Defensin against P. burhodogranariea was found.
source: We found activity of Diptericins against P. rettgeri, Drosocin against E. cloacae, Drosomycin and Metchnikowin against C. albicans, and Defensin against P. burhodogranariea.
evidence: This is supported by the survival data for these specific AMP-pathogen combinations.

claim: In most cases, the susceptibility of single mutants was slight.
source: In most cases, the susceptibility of single mutants was slight, and the contribution of individual AMPs could be revealed only when combined to other AMP mutations as illustrated by the susceptibility of Drosocin, Attacin, and Diptericin combined mutants to P. burhodogranariea.
evidence: This is supported by the survival data comparing single and compound mutants.

claim: The use of compound rather than single mutations provides a better strategy to decipher the contribution of AMPs to host defence.
source: Thus, the use of compound rather than single mutations provides a better strategy to decipher the contribution of AMPs to host defence.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that compound mutants often revealed effects not seen in single mutants.

claim: AMPs contribute greatly to resistance to Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Our study shows that AMPs contribute greatly to resistance to Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by the high susceptibility of ΔAMPs flies to Gram-negative bacteria.

claim: ΔAMPs flies are almost as susceptible as Imd-deficient mutants to most Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Consistent with this, ΔAMPs flies are almost as susceptible as Imd-deficient mutants to most Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of survival curves in Figure 2.

claim: Flies lacking AMPs were only slightly more susceptible to Gram-positive bacteria and fungal infections compared to wild-type flies.
source: In contrast, flies lacking AMPs were only slightly more susceptible to Gram-positive bacteria and fungal infections compared to wild-type flies, and this susceptibility rarely approached the susceptibility of Bomanin mutants.
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 2.

claim: The cell walls of Gram-negative bacteria are thinner and more fluid than the rigid cell walls of Gram-positive bacteria.
source: This may be due to the cell walls of Gram-negative bacteria being thinner and more fluid than the rigid cell walls of Gram-positive bacteria (Fayaz et al., 2010), consequently making Gram-negative bacteria more prone to the action of pore-forming cationic peptides.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Gram-negative bacteria are more prone to the action of pore-forming cationic peptides than Gram-positive bacteria.
source: This may be due to the cell walls of Gram-negative bacteria being thinner and more fluid than the rigid cell walls of Gram-positive bacteria (Fayaz et al., 2010), consequently making Gram-negative bacteria more prone to the action of pore-forming cationic peptides.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences in bacterial cell walls and supported by a citation.

claim: Mutations affecting Imd-pathway responsive antibacterial peptide genes are highly susceptible to Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Based on our study and Clemmons et al. (2015), we can now explain the susceptibility of Toll and Imd mutants at the level of the effectors, as we show that mutations affecting Imd-pathway responsive antibacterial peptide genes are highly susceptible to Gram-negative bacteria
evidence: This is supported by the survival data and a citation.

claim: The Toll-responsive targets Drosomycin, Metchnikowin, and especially the Bomanins, confer resistance to fungi and Gram-positive bacteria.
source: while the Toll-responsive targets Drosomycin, Metchnikowin, and especially the Bomanins, confer resistance to fungi and Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by the survival data.

claim: The susceptibility of Toll and Imd pathways to different sets of microbes reflects specificity at the level of recognition and can be translated to the activities of downstream effectors.
source: Thus, the susceptibility of these two pathways to different sets of microbes not only reflects specificity at the level of recognition, but can now also be translated to the activities of downstream effectors.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential susceptibility patterns of AMP and Bomanin mutants.

claim: Many putative effectors downstream of Toll and Imd remain uncharacterized.
source: It should also be noted that many putative effectors downstream of Toll and Imd remain uncharacterized, and so could also contribute to host defence beyond these AMPs and Bomanins.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the immune response complexity.

claim: Numerous in vitro studies have focused on the potential for synergistic interactions of AMPs in microbial killing.
source: In the last few years, numerous in vitro studies have focused on the potential for synergistic interactions of AMPs in microbial killing (Rahnamaeian et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2016; Zanchi et al., 2017; Yan and Hancock, 2001; Nuding et al., 2014; Zerweck et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2005; Stewart et al., 2014; Zdybicka-Barabas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Toll-responsive AMPs (Group C: Metchnikowin, Drosomycin) additively contributed to defence against the yeast C. albicans.
source: While Toll-responsive AMPs (Group C: Metchnikowin, Drosomycin) additively contributed to defence against the yeast C. albicans, we found that certain combinations of AMPs have synergistic contributions to defence against P. burhodogranariea.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: Certain combinations of AMPs have synergistic contributions to defence against P. burhodogranariea.
source: While Toll-responsive AMPs (Group C: Metchnikowin, Drosomycin) additively contributed to defence against the yeast C. albicans, we found that certain combinations of AMPs have synergistic contributions to defence against P. burhodogranariea.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: Co-occurring loss of Diptericins and Attacins led to complete loss of resistance to P. burhodogranariea.
source: This may be the case for the synergistic effect of Diptericins and Attacins against P. burhodogranariea, as only co-occurring loss of both these related glycine-rich peptide families (Hedengren et al., 2000) led to complete loss of resistance.
evidence: This is supported by survival data and a citation.

claim: The bumblebee AMP Abaecin binds to the molecular chaperone DnaK to inhibit bacterial DNA replication.
source: For instance, the action of the bumblebee AMP Abaecin, which binds to the molecular chaperone DnaK to inhibit bacterial DNA replication, is potentiated by the presence of the pore-forming peptide Hymenoptaecin (Rahnamaeian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The action of Abaecin is potentiated by the presence of the pore-forming peptide Hymenoptaecin.
source: For instance, the action of the bumblebee AMP Abaecin, which binds to the molecular chaperone DnaK to inhibit bacterial DNA replication, is potentiated by the presence of the pore-forming peptide Hymenoptaecin (Rahnamaeian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Drosophila Drosocin is highly similar to Abaecin and the related peptide Apidecin, including O-glycosylation of a critical threonine residue.
source: Drosophila Drosocin is highly similar to Abaecin and the related peptide Apidecin, including O-glycosylation of a critical threonine residue (Imler and Bulet, 2005; Hanson et al., 2016), and thus likely acts in a similar fashion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Drosocin likely acts in a similar fashion to Abaecin.
source: Drosophila Drosocin is highly similar to Abaecin and the related peptide Apidecin, including O-glycosylation of a critical threonine residue (Imler and Bulet, 2005; Hanson et al., 2016), and thus likely acts in a similar fashion.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity to Abaecin.

claim: Drosophila Attacin C is maturated into both a glycine-rich peptide and a Drosocin-like peptide called MPAC.
source: Furthermore, Drosophila Attacin C is maturated into both a glycine-rich peptide and a Drosocin-like peptide called MPAC (Rabel et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: It is commonly thought that the innate immune response lacks the specificity of the adaptive immune system.
source: It is commonly thought that the innate immune response lacks the specificity of the adaptive immune system, which mounts directed defences against specific pathogens.
evidence: This reflects a common view in immunology.

claim: The diversity of immune-inducible AMPs can be justified by the need for generalist and/or co-operative mechanisms of microbial killing.
source: Accordingly for innate immunity, the diversity of immune-inducible AMPs can be justified by the need for generalist and/or co-operative mechanisms of microbial killing.
evidence: This represents one hypothesis for AMP diversity.

claim: An alternate explanation for AMP diversity is that innate immunity expresses diverse AMPs in an attempt to hit the pathogen with a 'silver bullet:' an AMP specifically attuned to defend against that pathogen.
source: However, an alternate explanation may be that innate immunity expresses diverse AMPs in an attempt to hit the pathogen with a 'silver bullet:' an AMP specifically attuned to defend against that pathogen.
evidence: This represents an alternative hypothesis for AMP diversity.

claim: The study provides a demonstration in an in vivo setting that innate immunity may employ a 'silver bullet' strategy with specific AMPs.
source: Here, we provide a demonstration in an in vivo setting that such a strategy may actually be employed by the innate immune system.
evidence: This is supported by the specific AMP-pathogen interactions observed.

claim: Two examples of exquisite specificity were recovered in the relatively limited assays.
source: Remarkably, we recovered not just one, but two examples of exquisite specificity in our laborious but relatively limited assays.
evidence: This refers to the Diptericin-P. rettgeri and Drosocin-E. cloacae interactions.

claim: Diptericin has previously been highlighted for its important role in defence against P. rettgeri.
source: Diptericin has previously been highlighted for its important role in defence against P. rettgeri (Unckless et al., 2016), but it was previously unknown whether other AMPs may confer defence in this infection model.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Flies mutant for the other inducible AMPs resisted P. rettgeri infection as wild-type.
source: Astoundingly, flies mutant for the other inducible AMPs resisted P. rettgeri infection as wild-type, while only Diptericin mutants succumbed to infection.
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 5.

claim: Diptericins do not co-operate with other AMPs in defence against P. rettgeri and are solely responsible for defence in this specific host-pathogen interaction.
source: This means that Diptericins do not co-operate with these other AMPs in defence against P. rettgeri and are solely responsible for defence in this specific host-pathogen interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data showing only Diptericin mutants are susceptible.

claim: ~7 hpi appears to be the critical time point at which P. rettgeri either grows unimpeded or the infection is controlled.
source: A previous study has shown that ~7 hpi appears to be the critical time point at which P. rettgeri either grows unimpeded or the infection is controlled (Duneau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The critical time point of ~7 hpi correlates with the time at which the Diptericin transcriptional output is in full-force.
source: This time point correlates with the time at which the Diptericin transcriptional output is in full-force (Lemaitre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A lag in the transcriptional response in DptSK1/+ flies likely prevents the host from reaching a competent Diptericin concentration.
source: Thus, a lag in the transcriptional response in DptSK1/+ flies likely prevents the host from reaching a competent Diptericin concentration, indicating that Diptericin expression level is a key factor in successful host defence.
evidence: This is inferred from the heterozygote susceptibility and expression data.

claim: Diptericin expression level is a key factor in successful host defence against P. rettgeri.
source: Thus, a lag in the transcriptional response in DptSK1/+ flies likely prevents the host from reaching a competent Diptericin concentration, indicating that Diptericin expression level is a key factor in successful host defence.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-dependent susceptibility.

claim: Drosocin is specifically required for defence against E. cloacae.
source: We also show that Drosocin is specifically required for defence against E. cloacae.
evidence: This is supported by survival data in Figure 6.

claim: This finding validates previous biochemical analyses showing Drosocin in vitro activity against several Enterobacteriaceae, including E. cloacae.
source: This striking finding validates previous biochemical analyses showing Drosocin in vitro activity against several Enterobacteriaceae, including E. cloacae (Bulet et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Other AMPs also contribute to Drosocin-mediated control of E. cloacae.
source: As ΔAMPs flies are more susceptible than Drosocin single mutants, other AMPs also contribute to Drosocin-mediated control of E. cloacae.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in susceptibility between DroSK4 and ΔAMPs flies.

claim: Drosocin is similar to other Proline-rich AMPs (e.g. Abaecin, Pyrrhocoricin) that have been shown to target bacterial DnaK.
source: As highlighted above, Drosocin is similar to other Proline-rich AMPs (e.g. Abaecin, Pyrrhocoricin) that have been shown to target bacterial DnaK (Kragol et al., 2001; Rahnamaeian et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Proline-rich AMPs penetrate bacteria cell walls through their uptake by bacterial permeases.
source: Alone, these peptides still penetrate bacteria cell walls through their uptake by bacterial permeases (Rahnamaeian et al., 2016; Narayanan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Drosocin would benefit from the presence of pore-forming toxins to enter bacterial cells.
source: Thus, while Drosocin would benefit from the presence of pore-forming toxins to enter bacterial cells (Rahnamaeian et al., 2016), the veritable 'stake to the heart' is likely the plunging of Drosocin itself into vital bacterial machinery.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents an inference about mechanism.

claim: The plunging of Drosocin itself into vital bacterial machinery is likely the critical antimicrobial mechanism.
source: Thus, while Drosocin would benefit from the presence of pore-forming toxins to enter bacterial cells (Rahnamaeian et al., 2016), the veritable 'stake to the heart' is likely the plunging of Drosocin itself into vital bacterial machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific requirement for Drosocin and its similarity to other proline-rich AMPs.

claim: A common idea is that AMPs work as cocktails, wherein multiple effectors are needed to kill invading pathogens.
source: A common idea, supported by in vitro experiments (Rahnamaeian et al., 2015; Yan and Hancock, 2001; Zdybicka-Barabas et al., 2012) is that AMPs work as cocktails, wherein multiple effectors are needed to kill invading pathogens.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: The study finds support for an alternative hypothesis that AMP diversity may be due to highly specific interactions between AMPs and subsets of pathogens that they target.
source: However, we find support for an alternative hypothesis that suggests AMP diversity may be due to highly specific interactions between AMPs and subsets of pathogens that they target.
evidence: This is supported by the specific AMP-pathogen interactions observed.

claim: Drosophila and vertebrate AMPs experience positive selection.
source: Burgeoning support for this idea also comes from recent evolutionary studies that show Drosophila and vertebrate AMPs experience positive selection (Unckless et al., 2015; Unckless and Lazzaro, 2016; Hanson et al., 2016; Chapman et al., 2018; Hellgren and Sheldon, 2011; Tennessen and Blouin, 2008; Sackton, 2019), a hallmark of host-pathogen evolutionary conflict.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior evolutionary studies.

claim: Positive selection is a hallmark of host-pathogen evolutionary conflict.
source: Burgeoning support for this idea also comes from recent evolutionary studies that show Drosophila and vertebrate AMPs experience positive selection (Unckless et al., 2015; Unckless and Lazzaro, 2016; Hanson et al., 2016; Chapman et al., 2018; Hellgren and Sheldon, 2011; Tennessen and Blouin, 2008; Sackton, 2019), a hallmark of host-pathogen evolutionary conflict.
evidence: This is based on established evolutionary theory.

claim: AMP-pathogen specificity is fairly common.
source: Our functional demonstrations of AMP-pathogen specificity, using naturally relevant pathogens (Juneja and Lazzaro, 2009; Cox and Gilmore, 2007), suggest that such specificity is fairly common, and that certain AMPs can act as the arbiters of life or death upon infection by certain pathogens.
evidence: This is inferred from finding two specific interactions in a limited set of assays, supported by citations.

claim: Certain AMPs can act as the arbiters of life or death upon infection by certain pathogens.
source: Our functional demonstrations of AMP-pathogen specificity, using naturally relevant pathogens (Juneja and Lazzaro, 2009; Cox and Gilmore, 2007), suggest that such specificity is fairly common, and that certain AMPs can act as the arbiters of life or death upon infection by certain pathogens.
evidence: This is supported by the survival data showing specific AMP requirements.

claim: This stands in contrast to the classical view that the AMP response contains such redundancy that single peptides should have little effect on organism-level immunity.
source: This stands in contrast to the classical view that the AMP response contains such redundancy that single peptides should have little effect on organism-level immunity (Rolff and Schmid-Hempel, 2016; Unckless et al., 2015; Tzou et al., 2000; Unckless and Lazzaro, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior views in the literature.

claim: Immune effectors play non-redundant roles in defence.
source: Nevertheless, it seems these immune effectors play non-redundant roles in defence.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific AMP requirements observed.

claim: The study provides a long-awaited in vivo functional validation for the role of AMPs in host defence.
source: By providing a long-awaited in vivo functional validation for the role of AMPs in host defence, we also pave the way for a better understanding of the functions of immune effectors.
evidence: This summarizes the contribution of the study.

claim: The approach of using multiple compound mutants was especially effective to decipher the logic of immune effectors.
source: Our approach of using multiple compound mutants, now possible with the development of new genome editing approaches, was especially effective to decipher the logic of immune effectors.
evidence: This is inferred from the success of the compound mutant approach.

claim: Understanding the role of AMPs in innate immunity holds great promise for the development of novel antibiotics.
source: Understanding the role of AMPs in innate immunity holds great promise for the development of novel antibiotics (Chung et al., 2017; Mylonakis et al., 2016; Mahlapuu et al., 2016), insight into autoimmune diseases (Schluesener et al., 1993; Gilliet and Lande, 2008; Sun et al., 2015; Kumar et al., 2016), and given their potential for remarkably specific interactions, perhaps in predicting key parameters that predispose individuals or populations to certain kinds of infections (Unckless et al., 2015; Unckless and Lazzaro, 2016; Chapman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on AMP applications.

claim: The set of isogenized AMP mutant lines provides tools to decipher the role of AMPs in systemic immunity, local immune responses, aging, neurodegeneration, anti-tumor activity, and regulation of the microbiota.
source: Finally, our set of isogenized AMP mutant lines provides long-awaited tools to decipher the role of AMPs not only in systemic immunity, but also in local immune responses, and the various roles that AMPs may play in aging, neurodegeneration, anti-tumor activity, regulation of the microbiota and more, where disparate evidence has pointed to their involvement.
evidence: This describes the utility of the mutant lines for future research.
